lenses.lens: Shared mutable global state + thread safety in the exa and brave web-search client modules

findings.description: Check-then-act lazy init of the process-lifetime httpx.Client on module global _CLIENT is unsynchronized. Two threads entering _http() concurrently can both observe _CLIENT is None and both construct httpx.Client; the loser's client is discarded, leaving a closed/abandoned client with idle connections (small resource leak). No crash or wrong results.
findings.evidence:
exa/__init__.py:27 _CLIENT = None ; :31-40 def _http() -> "httpx.Client": """Process-lifetime client. Keep-alive pool; thread-safe for request()."""
    global _CLIENT
    if _CLIENT is None:
        _CLIENT = httpx.Client(limits=_ENGINE_LIMITS, follow_redirects=True, headers={"Accept": "application/json"})
    return _CLIENT
findings.suggestion: Guard with a module-level threading.Lock (double-checked locking) or pre-create the client at import time; keep the returned object immutable afterwards.

findings.description: Check-then-act lazy init of the process-lifetime ThreadPoolExecutor on module global _WORKERS is unsynchronized (same pattern as _CLIENT). A racy concurrent _pool() call leaks a second executor. Note: _fanout() (line 67) is DEAD CODE in exa — grep shows zero call sites outside its own definition, and no exa public function fans work out — so in exa this race is only reachable if a caller invokes the private _fanout/_pool from multiple threads; today it is effectively dormant.
findings.evidence:
exa/__init__.py:28 _WORKERS = None ; :43-47 def _pool(n: int = 8) -> ThreadPoolExecutor:
    global _WORKERS
    if _WORKERS is None:
        _WORKERS = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=n, thread_name_prefix="exa")
    return _WORKERS ; :67 def _fanout(jobs, *, concurrency: int = 8): ... :71 pool = _pool(max(8, int(concurrency or 8))) — and grep '_fanout(' in the exa file returns only line 67 (the def).
findings.suggestion: Guard with a module-level lock; or delete the unused _fanout/_pool/_WORKERS from exa (dead code) to remove the surface entirely.

findings.description: Module-level mutable dict _API_KEY_CACHE is read/written in _get_api_key() with an unsynchronized check-then-act: `if label in _API_KEY_CACHE: return ...` then `_API_KEY_CACHE[label] = key` after doing filesystem/env work. Under genuine multithreaded entry, several threads can miss the cache simultaneously, each run _seek_api_key() and each write the cache. Consequence is benign (identical value, atomic dict stores under the GIL, idempotent os.environ.setdefault), but it is a real data race on shared mutable state. In exa this path is only concurrent if an external caller threads the public functions, since exa's _fanout is dead code.
findings.evidence:
exa/__init__.py:409 _API_KEY_CACHE = {} ; :473-488 def _get_api_key():
    label = _API_LABEL
    if label in _API_KEY_CACHE:
        return _API_KEY_CACHE[label]
    key = _seek_api_key(_API_KEY_NAMES)
    ...
    for n in _API_KEY_NAMES:
        os.environ.setdefault(n, key)
    _API_KEY_CACHE[label] = key
    return key
findings.suggestion: Protect the check-then-act with a lock (or accept the race and document it as benign); also note the cache is process-lifetime: a rotated key in os.environ is never re-read once cached.

findings.description: Check-then-act lazy init of the process-lifetime ThreadPoolExecutor on module global _WORKERS, identical to exa — but UNLIKE exa it is live: _fanout() is called by real public entrypoints, so on the FIRST process-wide fanout call, N worker threads plus the main thread can all execute _pool() before any assignment lands. Losers' ThreadPoolExecutor instances leak (they were never used, so their worker threads exit at join/idle, but the object + file descriptors survive until GC). No wrong results: all callers use whichever executor they got.
findings.evidence:
brave/__init__.py:25 _WORKERS = None ; :39-43 def _pool(n: int = 8) -> ThreadPoolExecutor:
    global _WORKERS
    if _WORKERS is None:
        _WORKERS = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=n, thread_name_prefix="brave")
    return _WORKERS ; live call sites: :1982 _fanout([...web/news/video...], concurrency=3) inside search mode="all"; :3142 _fanout(jobs, concurrency=2) in thumbnails(); :3632 _fanout([...probe...], concurrency=8); :5424 _fanout(jobs, concurrency=4) in mosaic(); :5898 _fanout([...], concurrency=concurrency) in batch().
findings.suggestion: Guard with a module-level lock, or eagerly create the pool at import / first main-thread call (e.g., in module __init__) so the init path is single-threaded.

findings.description: Module-level mutable dict _API_KEY_CACHE is checked and written in _get_api_key() with check-then-act, and in brave this IS reached concurrently by real worker threads: every _fanout thunk calls _request() -> _get_api_key(). On the first fanout call with a cold cache (no BRAVE_API_KEY pre-exported, key found via dotenv/key-file), all N worker threads (concurrency up to 8 in crawl, 4 in mosaic, 3 in mode=all) pass `if label in _API_KEY_CACHE` before any write, each performs the full _seek_api_key() filesystem walk in parallel, and each executes `_API_KEY_CACHE[label] = key` concurrently. Consequence is still benign in practice (deterministic identical value, GIL-atomic dict stores, idempotent setdefault) — no crash/wrong key — but this is the one module-global in the audit that is actually read-modify-written by concurrently spawned threads as a matter of normal operation, not just in theory.
findings.suggestion: Resolve the key once in the main thread before building jobs (e.g., key = _get_api_key() in batch()/mosaic()/crawl() and pass it to the thunks), or guard the cache check-then-act with a lock; consider invalidating the cache on 401 so a rotated key is picked up.

findings.description: Both modules expose one process-lifetime httpx.Client (global _CLIENT, lazy-init at exa:34 / brave:30) and its docstring asserts 'thread-safe for request()'. httpx's own documentation states a Client is not safe for CONCURRENT use of .close() while requests are in flight; brave in particular drives concurrent request() calls through its _fanout pool (up to 8 in parallel in crawl()). If any actor calls _CLIENT.close() (cleanup hook, test teardown, an embedding host) while fanout workers are mid-request, workers raise RuntimeError('Cannot close a client instance which is still in use') and every subsequent search in the process fails permanently — the global is never re-created. The modules never call close() themselves, so this is a latent contract drift on the shared global, not an in-module bug.
findings.evidence:
exa/__init__.py:31-40 def _http() -> "httpx.Client":
    """Process-lifetime client. Keep-alive pool; thread-safe for request()."""
    global _CLIENT
    if _CLIENT is None:
        _CLIENT = httpx.Client(limits=_ENGINE_LIMITS, ...)
    return _CLIENT — brave/__init__.py:27-36 is byte-identical (follow_redirects=False); concurrent use is live in brave via :3632 _fanout([...probe...], concurrency=8) where each thunk does _http().get(...).
findings.suggestion: Remove the blanket 'thread-safe' claim and document the close() hazard; or return a fresh request context (httpx use as contextmanager) when concurrency is active, or serialize close() with the same lock used for lazy init.

lenses.summary: Both modules carry the same three module-level mutable globals: _CLIENT (lazy httpx.Client), _WORKERS (lazy process-lifetime ThreadPoolExecutor), and _API_KEY_CACHE (dict). All mutations are unsynchronized check-then-act patterns, but none is exploitable into a crash or wrong results under CPython's GIL: _CLIENT/_WORKERS races merely create a discarded duplicate object (leak), and the _API_KEY_CACHE race re-runs a deterministic, idempotent key lookup and writes the same value. Thread usage is asymmetric: brave's _fanout is live (search mode=all :1982, thumbnails :3142, crawl :3632, mosaic :5424, batch :5898), so on a cold first fanout call _WORKERS, _CLIENT, and _API_KEY_CACHE are all touched by concurrently spawned worker threads — the _API_KEY_CACHE check-then-act under real concurrency is the most significant finding, though still benign (parallel redundant key discovery, not corruption). In exa, _fanout/_pool/_WORKERS are dead code (zero call sites), so its lazy-init races are only theoretical unless an external caller threads the public functions; exa's _get_api_key is then only ever hit sequentially per process. All other top-level collections (PATHS, MODES, LOC_HEADERS, VALID_CATEGORIES, SEARCH_TYPES, _STOPWORDS, _ENTITY_PROFILE_KEYS, _KIND_SCHEMA, _UNITCONV_FACTORS, _RICH_VERTICALS, _DOC_DOMAINS, etc.) are verified read-only after import — no runtime .update/.append/index-assignment found — and _fanout deliberately collects via per-future results rather than a shared output dict, so there is no shared-dict write race. The one genuine contract concern is the shared _CLIENT's 'thread-safe for request()' docstring (both, exa:32/brave:28), which omits httpx's documented hazard of concurrent close(); a premature close while brave's fanout is in flight would poison every subsequent call process-wide. Net assessment: no critical or high-severity data races; the state is shared but effectively race-harmless, with one medium live cache-race surface in brave and two low-severity structural smells duplicated across both modules.

The dual sync/async wrapper design (exa:129-335, brave:495-723) is functionally sound for the primary use case — `await fn(...)` on a dict/str/list/None works, and sync callers keep working because the wrappers subclass the built-ins. The bool-before-int ordering in _wrap_result is correct for plain values. However, the mechanism has several verified defects rooted in one structural flaw: because all six _Async* wrappers subclass their built-in (and _AsyncBool subclasses int, not bool), the `hasattr(value, "__await__")` "return untouched" guard in _wrap_result is dead code — the isinstance checks always match first, so an already-wrapped value is silently re-wrapped into a NEW object instead of returned as-is. This makes wrapping non-idempotent and demotes a re-wrapped _AsyncBool to _AsyncInt. The _apply_async_to guard `__name__=="_async_aware"` is likewise dead because functools.wraps copies the original __name__. Additionally, _apply_async_to(globals()) wraps EVERY public module name that is a FunctionType, including the stdlib-imported parsedate_to_datetime, whose datetime return becomes a _AsyncScalar proxy that breaks datetime arithmetic. Awaiting is also asymmetric: containers yield shallow copies (top-level detached, nested objects still shared) while scalars/result-classes yield the live object, contradicting the module's "await yields the SAME real result" contract and giving sync-vs-async callers different aliasing semantics. No public function currently returns a bare bool or None, so the demotion and None-identity defects are latent/low-impact today but are real edge cases.

findings.description: The `hasattr(value, "__await__"): return value` guard in _wrap_result is dead code. Because _AsyncDict/_AsyncStr/_AsyncList/_AsyncInt/_AsyncFloat/_AsyncBool all subclass their built-in base type, the isinstance checks at the top of _wrap_result (dict/str/list/bool/int/float) always match an already-wrapped value BEFORE the guard is reached. As a result an already-wrapped value is re-wrapped into a brand-new wrapper object instead of being returned untouched, making wrapping non-idempotent and defeating the 'return untouched' contract the guard documents.
findings.evidence: exa:216-235 (brave:605-624). Verified: `wd=exa._wrap_result({'a':1}); exa._wrap_result(wd) is wd` -> False (new _AsyncDict created, guard never fires). All six wrapper instances have __await__ yet each still matches its base isinstance branch first (dict/str/list/bool->int/float). The guard only ever catches _AsyncScalar (which has no base isinstance match) and result classes that already define __await__.
findings.suggestion: Check `hasattr(value, "__await__")` FIRST (before the isinstance chain) so already-wrapped / awaitable values are returned as-is, or re-wrap only when `type(value)` is exactly a built-in (type(value) is dict/str/list/int/float/bool) so subclasses pass through.

findings.description: __await__ returns inconsistent kinds of value across the wrapper set: containers (dict/str/list) and primitives (int/float/bool) return a COPY, while _AsyncScalar and the result classes (via _identity_await) return the LIVE object. This contradicts the module docstring's claim that awaiting yields 'the SAME real result', and produces asymmetric aliasing: a sync caller mutating the top-level of a dict sees the change, but the async (awaited) copy does not; conversely a sync caller of a result class and the awaited value are the SAME object. Dict/list copies are also only SHALLOW — nested objects are shared, so post-await mutation of a nested value leaks into the 'copied' result.
findings.evidence: exa:144-147 (_AsyncDict.__await__ -> `return dict(self)`), 164-167 (_AsyncList -> `list(self)`); exa:246-249 (_AsyncScalar.__await__ -> `return self._v` = live object); exa:133-137 (_identity_await -> `return self`); exa:5984-5986 (result classes get _identity_await). Verified: `await _AsyncDict` -> new dict not the wrapper, but `aw['nested'] is orig['nested']` is True (shallow); `await _AsyncScalar(obj) is obj` -> True; `await SearchResults is self` -> True. Docstring exa:108-110: 'value = await fn(...) -> the SAME real result'.
findings.suggestion: Pick one semantics and state it: either always return the live instance (so `await x is x` uniformly True and docstring holds) or always return a deep-ish copy, and document that nested objects are shared. Do not mix copy and live semantics for 'the same' await operation.

findings.description: _AsyncBool subclasses int (not bool) and defines __new__ via int.__new__(cls, bool(v)), so an _AsyncBool is NOT an instance of bool. Combined with the dead __await__ guard, re-wrapping an _AsyncBool falls into the `isinstance(value, int)` branch of _wrap_result and demotes it to _AsyncInt — awaiting then yields 1/0 (int) instead of True/False, and __str__/__repr__ lose their bool override. Currently latent because no public function returns a bare bool (all public bool-returning logic is folded into dict results), but it is a real demotion the moment a public func returns a bool.
findings.evidence: exa:196-213 (class _AsyncBool(int): def __new__(cls,v): return int.__new__(cls, bool(v))); exa:224-227 (bool check then int check in _wrap_result). Verified: `type(exa._AsyncBool(True)).__name__=='_AsyncBool'`; `isinstance(exa._AsyncBool(True), bool)` -> False; `type(exa._wrap_result(exa._AsyncBool(True))).__name__` -> '_AsyncInt'; `await` of the re-wrap -> 1 (int) instead of True.
findings.suggestion: Make _AsyncBool subclass bool, or add an explicit `isinstance(value, _AsyncBool)` (and the other wrapper types) short-circuit at the top of _wrap_result so re-wrapping a wrapper is a no-op rather than a demotion.

findings.description: The guard `if getattr(_obj, "__name__", "") == "_async_aware": continue` in _apply_async_to is dead code. _make_async builds the twin with @functools.wraps(fn), which copies the ORIGINAL function's __name__ onto the wrapper, so no wrapped function ever has __name__ == '_async_aware' (they keep the public name, e.g. 'search'). The guard can never match, so a second call to _apply_async_to on an already-wrapped globals dict would re-wrap each public function rather than skip it.
findings.evidence: exa:329-330 (brave:718-719): `if getattr(_obj, "__name__", "") == "_async_aware": continue`. Verified: `w = exa._make_async(lambda:1); w.__name__` -> '<lambda>' (the wrapped fn's original name), never '_async_aware'. Because _apply_async_to runs once at import there is no observable bug today, but the guard provides false assurance and would silently double-wrap on re-application.
findings.suggestion: Guard on a stable marker instead of __name__ (e.g. set a custom attribute like `fn.__wrapped_by__ = 'async_aware'` in _make_async and check it, or check `getattr(_obj, '__wrapped__', None) is not None`).

findings.description: _apply_async_to(globals()) wraps EVERY public module name that is a types.FunctionType, with no filter for functions that were merely IMPORTED rather than defined in the module. `parsedate_to_datetime` (imported from email.utils at module level) is therefore wrapped into an async-aware twin that is exposed as a public module attribute AND is what the internal _retry_after_seconds call site uses. Its datetime return is boxed in _AsyncScalar, so internal code receives a proxied datetime instead of a real one; `.timestamp()` happens to work (proxied via __getattr__) but other datetime ops raise TypeError, making _retry_after_seconds depend on the proxy's partial surface rather than the real type.
findings.evidence: exa:24 `from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime`; exa:61 internal call `dt = parsedate_to_datetime(raw)`; exa:334 `module_dict[_name] = _make_async(_obj)` (brave:21, brave:58, brave:723). Verified: `exa.parsedate_to_datetime` is wrapped; calling it returns `type == _AsyncScalar` (repr datetime(...)); `(wrapped_date) - timedelta(seconds=1)` -> TypeError (only __getattr__ methods like .timestamp() are proxied).
findings.suggestion: Restrict wrapping to functions defined in this module (e.g. `if getattr(_obj, '__module__', None) != <this module>: continue`), and import stdlib helpers with a leading-underscore alias so they stay private. Same fix prevents any future `from X import Y` from being silently re-exported as a wrapped public callable.

findings.description: None pass-through is a contract drift. A public function that returns None is boxed in _AsyncScalar(None); the sync caller then receives the proxy, not None, so `result is None` is False (only `not result` is truthy). _AsyncScalar also defers __iter__/__getitem__/__len__/__contains__ straight to None, so those raise TypeError/AttributeError rather than a clean None. Currently latent: no public function in either module returns a bare None (a targeted scan of all wrapped public funcs found none), so this is a latent edge case rather than an active bug — but it will silently break the moment a public fn adds a 'return None' and any caller tests `is None`.
findings.evidence: exa:234-235 / exa:238-261 (_wrap_result fallback `return _AsyncScalar(value)` 'incl. None'; _AsyncScalar.__iter__ -> iter(self._v), __len__ -> len(self._v)). Verified: `w=exa._wrap_result(None); type(w)=='_AsyncScalar'; w is None -> False; bool(w) -> False; iter(w) -> TypeError('NoneType' object is not iterable)`. Scan of all wrapped public functions in exa and brave found no top-level 'return None'.
findings.suggestion: Return None (and ideally other identity-sensitive singletons) untouched from _wrap_result, i.e. add `if value is None: return value` before the generic fallback, so `await fn()` and `fn()` both give exactly None and `is None` checks keep working.

lenses.summary: The auth-key plumbing is shared nearly verbatim between the two modules (exa 407-488, brave 886-967). No credential is ever interpolated into logs, error messages, or returned strings: the key is only placed in the `x-api-key` / `X-Subscription-Token` header (exa 508, 2652, 2758, 2860; brave 982, 4609) and the 401/422/5xx error text interpolates only the response `detail`/`body`, the `path`, and query `params` — never the key or the header dict; the only `print` is exa 1283 (a category warning). So I report no leak finding. There are, however, three substantiated defects in the key-resolution path: (1) a process-lifetime `_API_KEY_CACHE` that is never invalidated, so a corrected/rotated key in the environment or a key file is not picked up in-process — which directly defeats the modules' own 401 remediation text and matters for the persistent IPython agent kernel exa explicitly targets; (2) key-store files (e.g. `~/.prime/agent/keys/exa.key`, `secrets.env`) are ALWAYS parsed by the hand-rolled `_read_key_file` (naive `.strip("'\"")`, no inline-comment handling, `len>=12` bare-token heuristic) even when `python-dotenv` is installed, since dotenv is used only for the env-file list; (3) `os.environ.setdefault` mutates the process environment as a side effect, and in brave the two-name priority lets a stale `BRAVE_API_KEY` shadow a correct `BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY`.

findings.description: _API_KEY_CACHE is written once per label and never invalidated (no .clear()/.pop()/del anywhere in either module). Once a key is resolved, all later calls in the same process return the cached value and never re-read the environment or key files. A user who rotates/fixes the key mid-process (re-export EXA_API_KEY/BRAVE_API_KEY, or edit the key file) gets the SAME stale key on every subsequent call, so 401s persist and the documented recovery ('export a fresh EXA_API_KEY', 're-export', 're-run /login') silently does not work in-process. This is biting for the intended runtime: exa's docstring (lines 112-113) targets a long-lived IPython agent kernel that reuses the module across many await skill.search(...) calls.
findings.evidence: exa/src/exa/__init__.py:475-487  if label in _API_KEY_CACHE: return _API_KEY_CACHE[label]; key = _seek_api_key(_API_KEY_NAMES); ... _API_KEY_CACHE[label] = key; return key   ||  brave/src/brave/__init__.py:954-966 (identical). 401 guidance that becomes dead-on-arrival: exa:528 'Your EXA_API_KEY is invalid, expired, or revoked. Re-run /login (choose exa) or export a fresh EXA_API_KEY.' There is no _API_KEY_CACHE.clear()/pop()/del anywhere (grep confirmed only init at exa:409 / brave:888 and the read/write above).
findings.suggestion: Make the cache a negative-key-safe memo that re-reads when the underlying source changes, or drop the module-level cache and resolve per call (env lookup is cheap). If keeping the cache, expose an invalidate() and document that re-exporting requires a process restart.

findings.description: Key-store files (~/.prime/agent/keys/exa.key, exa_search_api_key.key, secrets.env, ~/.prime/keys/exa.env, ~/.exa.env — and the PRIME_DOTENV/env files when the dotenv branch misses) are ALWAYS parsed by the naive _read_key_file, never by python-dotenv: the dotenv branch (exa:430-438 / brave:908-917) iterates only the short `files` env-file list, and even when dotenv is installed it is not applied to the key-store files. Consequences for those files: (a) inline comments are not stripped — `EXA_API_KEY=abc # note` yields `abc # note`; (b) `.strip("'\"")` mangles unbalanced quotes ('abc -> abc, "abc -> abc, and strips ALL leading/trailing quote chars); (c) the `len>=12 and "/" not in line` bare-token heuristic treats the first preamble/metadata line that has no '=' and no '/' as the key, a false positive when a key-store file has a header line (>=12 chars) above the real token. python-dotenv is not a declared dependency (both pyproject.toml list only httpx), so the naive parser is the live path in most deployments.
findings.evidence: exa/src/exa/__init__.py:453-471 / brave:932-950  _read_key_file: ... if '=' in line: k,_,v = line.partition('='); if k.strip() in names and v.strip(): return v.strip().strip("'\"")  elif len(line) >= 12 and '/' not in line and line not in names: return line.strip().strip("'\"")   ||  dotenv used only for env files: exa:430-438 `for p in files: ... return d[n].strip()` (no quote-strip), then exa:447-450 falls through to `for p in key_files: v=_read_key_file(p,names)` (key_files = 5 key-store paths + files). Same shape at brave:908-930.
findings.suggestion: Route key-store files through the same parser used for env files (or always use python-dotenv when available, declaring it a dependency) so quoting/comment handling is consistent; gate the bare-token heuristic on the whole file being a single token (e.g. no other K=V lines present) to avoid preamble false positives.

findings.description: _get_api_key mutates the process environment as a side effect of reading a key: for every key name it runs os.environ.setdefault(n, key), writing the found key into the env even when the user only configured it via a key file or via the *other* name. In brave, _API_KEY_NAMES=['BRAVE_API_KEY','BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY'] and _seek_api_key checks them in order, so a stale BRAVE_API_KEY in the env shadows a correct BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY (first name wins), and setdefault then also pins BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY to that stale value; combined with the never-invalidated cache, unsetting one variable later does not help. Exa (single name) has the same env-mutation smell in a milder form. This is a state-mutation surprise for a library whose only job is to search.
findings.evidence: exa/src/exa/__init__.py:485-486 `for n in _API_KEY_NAMES: os.environ.setdefault(n, key)` (names=['EXA_API_KEY'])  ||  brave/src/brave/__init__.py:964-965 `for n in _API_KEY_NAMES: os.environ.setdefault(n, key)` with 886 `_API_KEY_NAMES = ['BRAVE_API_KEY', 'BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY']` and 893-896 env lookup that returns the first matching name.
findings.suggestion: Do not write back to os.environ from a library (remove the setdefault loop); if a downstream tool genuinely needs the var, document that. For brave, prefer the env var the user actually set over an older sibling, or at least don't cross-populate the two names.

lenses.summary:
Both clients share a near-identical clean-engine skeleton (process-lifetime httpx.Client with Limits(max_connections=16), a lazy module-global _pool, an identical _retry_after_seconds that correctly honors Retry-After in both seconds and date form and clamps to [0.05, 8.0], and an _fanout that submits all jobs first then collects). The Retry-After handling is correct in both. The substantive issues are asymmetric between the two modules.

Brave's _request is the more defensive of the two: it explicitly catches httpx.TimeoutException/ConnectError/ConnectTimeout/ReadTimeout, retries 429/5xx and even "200-but-non-JSON", and fast-fails on auth/validation. Its one real defect is the fallback path: _run_fallback returns None when the fallback endpoint also fails, and the sole caller (_search_full, local mode) hands that None straight to _query_diag, which does data.get(...) -> AttributeError.

Exa's _request is the weaker one: it only classifies HTTP status codes and does NOT catch any transport-level httpx exception, so a ConnectError/ReadTimeout/PoolTimeout (very common on a 45s timeout for heavy deep-reasoning/answer/search calls) raises a raw httpx exception with no retry — directly contradicting its docstring claim that "transient failures are retried." It also re-sends non-idempotent stateful POST/PATCH requests on 429/5xx, risking duplicate agent runs/monitors/websets (double billing), and its success-path resp.json() is unguarded. Both modules also share an unlocked check-then-set lazy init for the shared Client and thread pool, which contradicts the docstring "thread-safe" claim under concurrent first use.

Design note (not reported as a bug): Brave's HTTP-transient backoff is linear (1.0*attempt), not exponential, whereas Exa's no-header fallback is exponential (2**attempt*0.5); both are clamped to 8.0s by _retry_after_seconds.

findings.description: Fallback path can crash with AttributeError. _run_fallback (lines 1059-1075) returns None in several cases (fallback GET raises, alt.status_code != 200 at lines 1068-1069, or alt.json() fails at 1071-1073). _request then does `return _run_fallback(...)` at line 1044, so _request returns None. The only caller that passes fallback= is _search_full at line 2010 (`data = _request(path, params, timeout, fallback=fallback, ...)`), which immediately calls `diag = _query_diag(data)` at line 2011 with data=None; _query_diag line 1716 does `q = data.get("query") or {}` -> AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get'.
findings.evidence: line 1044: `return _run_fallback(fallback, params, headers, timeout, path, resp.status_code)`; line 1068-1069: `if alt.status_code != 200:\n        return None`; line 2010: `data = _request(path, params, timeout, fallback=fallback, headers=loc_headers)`; line 2011: `diag = _query_diag(data)`; line 1716: `q = data.get("query") or {}`
findings.suggestion: In _search_full, guard the fallback return: `data = _request(...)` then `if data is None: raise BraveError('local search failed and web fallback also failed')` before calling _query_diag; or make _request re-raise the original transient error instead of returning None when the fallback yields nothing.

findings.description: exa._request does not catch any transport-level httpx exception. The request call at line 507 is not wrapped in try/except, so httpx.ConnectError/ConnectTimeout/ReadTimeout/PoolTimeout propagate out of _request as raw httpx exceptions with NO retry. This contradicts the docstring (lines 502-500) that 'Transient failures (429 rate-limit, 5xx) are retried up to _retries times with short exponential backoff so a single throttled call does not kill a fan-out.' Only 4xx/5xx status codes (line 518) are retried; a slow response (ReadTimeout at the 45s/60s/90s timeouts used by search/answer/agent) or a connection blip is not retried and surfaces as an unhandled exception to every public caller (search, run, answer, agent, ...).
findings.evidence: lines 506-508: `for attempt in range(_retries + 1):\n        resp = _http().request(method, url, params=params, json=json_body,\n                               headers={"x-api-key": api_key}, timeout=timeout)` (no surrounding try/except); contrast brave lines 991-1008 which wrap the request in `try: ... except (httpx.TimeoutException, httpx.ConnectError, httpx.ConnectTimeout, httpx.ReadTimeout)`.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the _http().request(...) call in try/except for (httpx.TimeoutException, httpx.ConnectError, httpx.ConnectTimeout, httpx.ReadTimeout, httpx.PoolTimeout) and treat it like a transient failure: sleep(_retry_after_seconds(None, 2**attempt*0.5)) and continue within the attempt loop, raising a clean ExaError after exhausting attempts.

findings.description: Non-idempotent stateful requests are blindly re-sent on 429/5xx. _request retries (lines 518-520) apply to every method, including state-creating POST/PATCH/DELETE calls: POST /agent/runs (line 2404, charges agent compute), POST /monitors (line 2998), POST /v0/websets (line 3384), PATCH /monitors/{id} (3019/3216/3917/4014/4018), POST /v0/imports (3950), etc. If a 5xx is returned after the server has already created the resource (or a POST is retried after a 429), the resource can be created twice / billed twice. Even the read endpoints POST /search, /answer, /contents bill per call, so a retried 5xx doubles cost.
findings.evidence: lines 518-520: `if status in (429, 500, 502, 503, 504) and attempt < _retries:\n            time.sleep(_retry_after_seconds(resp, 2 ** attempt * 0.5))\n            continue` (applies regardless of method); line 2404: `created = _request("POST", "/agent/runs", key, json_body=body, timeout=min(timeout, 30))`
findings.suggestion: Only auto-retry idempotent requests, or make _request accept an idempotency signal; for stateful POST/PATCH/DELETE, retry 5xx only when the response indicates the request was not processed, and/or send a client-generated idempotency key on mutating endpoints.

findings.description: Lazy init of the shared process-lifetime httpx.Client and the shared ThreadPoolExecutor is an unlocked check-then-set on a module global, despite the docstring claiming 'thread-safe for request()'. Under concurrent first use (brave batch()/mode='all' _fanout and exa fan-out all submit thread-pool thunks that call _request->_http() at once), two threads can both observe _CLIENT is None and each construct a Client (leaking one, doubling the 16-connection pool briefly); the same pattern applies to _WORKERS, leaking a ThreadPoolExecutor with live threads.
findings.suggestion: Guard lazy init with a module-level threading.Lock (create-once under the lock, then re-check the global), or eagerly create _CLIENT/_WORKERS at import time so the check-then-set race disappears.

findings.description: Success-path resp.json() is unguarded. On a 2xx response exa does `return resp.json()` with no try/except, so a 2xx with an empty or non-JSON body raises a raw JSONDecodeError out of _request to every caller. Note the failure path right below (lines 512-515) DOES guard resp.json(), so only the success path is exposed; brave explicitly handles the analogous '200-but-unparseable' case as a transient retry (brave lines 1017-1025), exa does not.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the success-path resp.json() in try/except and, on failure, treat it as a transient server-side oddity (retry within the attempt loop) before surfacing a clean ExaError.

lenses.lens: CROSS-MODULE SHARED CODE: exa vs brave helper duplication
lenses.summary: The two modules share large, near-identical plumbing copied verbatim or with only trivial renames. Verified by line-range diffs: (1) a ~200-line dual sync/async wrapper set (exa 133-334, brave 522-723) that is BYTE-IDENTICAL, including the module-tail `_apply_async_to(globals())` hook (exa:5988, brave:7213); (2) a ~80-line API-key lookup trio `_seek_api_key`/`_read_key_file`/`_get_api_key` (exa 411-488, brave 890-967) that is BYTE-IDENTICAL (only the `_API_KEY_NAMES`/`_API_LABEL` constants differ, which is the intended parameterization); (3) the HTTP-engine core `_http/_pool/_retry_after_seconds/_fanout` plus the module globals `_ENGINE_LIMITS/_CLIENT/_WORKERS` (exa 26-79, brave 23-80) that differ only by trivial renames (`follow_redirects=True/False`, `thread_name_prefix="exa"/"brave"`, docstrings). These three are strong candidates for lifting into an internal `_common` module; the only intended differences are the redirect flag, the worker-name prefix, and the key-name/label constants, all of which would need to be parameterized. By contrast, the domain/url helpers are DIVERGENT (exa `_domain_of` is a registrable-domain label-slicer; brave `_url_host` is a hostname+www-strip) and should NOT be merged. Also note `_request` is NOT near-identical (exa POST + x-api-key + ExaError taxonomy; brave GET + X-Subscription-Token + BraveError taxonomy + fallback endpoints) and shares only the engine primitives, so a `_common` lift should stop at the engine. exa additionally has `_poll_until` (82-100) with no brave counterpart. findings.description: Both modules expose one process-lifetime httpx.Client (global _CLIENT, lazy-init at exa:34 / brave:30) and its docstring asserts 'thread-safe for request()'. httpx's own documentation states a Client is not safe for CONCURRENT use of .close() while requests are in flight; brave in particular drives concurrent request() calls through its _fanout pool (up to 8 in parallel in crawl()). If any actor calls _CLIENT.close() (cleanup hook, test teardown, an embedding host) while fanout workers are mid-request, workers raise RuntimeError('Cannot close a client instance which is still in use') and every subsequent search in the process fails permanently — the global is never re-created. The modules never call close() themselves, so this is a latent contract drift on the shared global, not an in-module bug.

    """Process-lifetime client. Keep-alive pool; thread-safe for request()."""

findings.suggestion: Remove the blanket 'thread-safe' claim and document the close() hazard; or return a fresh request context (httpx use as contextmanager) when concurrency is active, or serialize close() with the same lock used for lazy init.

findings.lens: DUAL SYNC/ASYNC RESULT WRAPPERS
findings.description: The `hasattr(value, "__await__"): return value` guard in _wrap_result is dead code. Because _AsyncDict/_AsyncStr/_AsyncList/_AsyncInt/_AsyncFloat/_AsyncBool all subclass their built-in base type, the isinstance checks at the top of _wrap_result (dict/str/list/bool/int/float) always match an already-wrapped value BEFORE the guard is reached. As a result an already-wrapped value is re-wrapped into a brand-new wrapper object instead of being returned untouched, making wrapping non-idempotent and defeating the 'return untouched' contract the guard documents.
findings.evidence: exa:216-235 (brave:605-624). Verified: `wd=exa._wrap_result({'a':1}); exa._wrap_result(wd) is wd` -> False (new _AsyncDict created, guard never fires). All six wrapper instances have __await__ yet each still matches its base isinstance branch first (dict/str/list/bool->int/float). The guard only ever catches _AsyncScalar (which has no base isinstance match) and result classes that already define __await__.
findings.suggestion: Check `hasattr(value, "__await__")` FIRST (before the isinstance chain) so already-wrapped / awaitable values are returned as-is, or re-wrap only when `type(value)` is exactly a built-in (type(value) is dict/str/list/int/float/bool) so subclasses pass through.

findings.lens: DUAL SYNC/ASYNC RESULT WRAPPERS
findings.description: __await__ returns inconsistent kinds of value across the wrapper set: containers (dict/str/list) and primitives (int/float/bool) return a COPY, while _AsyncScalar and the result classes (via _identity_await) return the LIVE object. This contradicts the module docstring's claim that awaiting yields 'the SAME real result', and produces asymmetric aliasing: a sync caller mutating the top-level of a dict sees the change, but the async (awaited) copy does not; conversely a sync caller of a result class and the awaited value are the SAME object. Dict/list copies are also only SHALLOW — nested objects are shared, so post-await mutation of a nested value leaks into the 'copied' result.
findings.evidence: exa:144-147 (_AsyncDict.__await__ -> `return dict(self)`), 164-167 (_AsyncList -> `list(self)`); exa:246-249 (_AsyncScalar.__await__ -> `return self._v` = live object); exa:133-137 (_identity_await -> `return self`); exa:5984-5986 (result classes get _identity_await). Verified: `await _AsyncDict` -> new dict not the wrapper, but `aw['nested'] is orig['nested']` is True (shallow); `await _AsyncScalar(obj) is obj` -> True; `await SearchResults is self` -> True. Docstring exa:108-110: 'value = await fn(...) -> the SAME real result'.
findings.suggestion: Pick one semantics and state it: either always return the live instance (so `await x is x` uniformly True and docstring holds) or always return a deep-ish copy, and document that nested objects are shared. Do not mix copy and live semantics for 'the same' await operation.

findings.lens: DUAL SYNC/ASYNC RESULT WRAPPERS
findings.description: _AsyncBool subclasses int (not bool) and defines __new__ via int.__new__(cls, bool(v)), so an _AsyncBool is NOT an instance of bool. Combined with the dead __await__ guard, re-wrapping an _AsyncBool falls into the `isinstance(value, int)` branch of _wrap_result and demotes it to _AsyncInt — awaiting then yields 1/0 (int) instead of True/False, and __str__/__repr__ lose their bool override. Currently latent because no public function returns a bare bool (all public bool-returning logic is folded into dict results), but it is a real demotion the moment a public func returns a bool.
findings.evidence: exa:196-213 (class _AsyncBool(int): def __new__(cls,v): return int.__new__(cls, bool(v))); exa:224-227 (bool check then int check in _wrap_result). Verified: `type(exa._AsyncBool(True)).__name__=='_AsyncBool'`; `isinstance(exa._AsyncBool(True), bool)` -> False; `type(exa._wrap_result(exa._AsyncBool(True))).__name__` -> '_AsyncInt'; `await` of the re-wrap -> 1 (int) instead of True.
findings.suggestion: Make _AsyncBool subclass bool, or add an explicit `isinstance(value, _AsyncBool)` (and the other wrapper types) short-circuit at the top of _wrap_result so re-wrapping a wrapper is a no-op rather than a demotion.

findings.lens: DUAL SYNC/ASYNC RESULT WRAPPERS
findings.description: The guard `if getattr(_obj, "__name__", "") == "_async_aware": continue` in _apply_async_to is dead code. _make_async builds the twin with @functools.wraps(fn), which copies the ORIGINAL function's __name__ onto the wrapper, so no wrapped function ever has __name__ == '_async_aware' (they keep the public name, e.g. 'search'). The guard can never match, so a second call to _apply_async_to on an already-wrapped globals dict would re-wrap each public function rather than skip it.
findings.evidence: exa:329-330 (brave:718-719): `if getattr(_obj, "__name__", "") == "_async_aware": continue`. Verified: `w = exa._make_async(lambda:1); w.__name__` -> '<lambda>' (the wrapped fn's original name), never '_async_aware'. Because _apply_async_to runs once at import there is no observable bug today, but the guard provides false assurance and would silently double-wrap on re-application.
findings.suggestion: Guard on a stable marker instead of __name__ (e.g. set a custom attribute like `fn.__wrapped_by__ = 'async_aware'` in _make_async and check it, or check `getattr(_obj, '__wrapped__', None) is not None`).

findings.lens: DUAL SYNC/ASYNC RESULT WRAPPERS
findings.description: _apply_async_to(globals()) wraps EVERY public module name that is a types.FunctionType, with no filter for functions that were merely IMPORTED rather than defined in the module. `parsedate_to_datetime` (imported from email.utils at module level) is therefore wrapped into an async-aware twin that is exposed as a public module attribute AND is what the internal _retry_after_seconds call site uses. Its datetime return is boxed in _AsyncScalar, so internal code receives a proxied datetime instead of a real one; `.timestamp()` happens to work (proxied via __getattr__) but other datetime ops raise TypeError, making _retry_after_seconds depend on the proxy's partial surface rather than the real type.
findings.evidence: exa:24 `from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime`; exa:61 internal call `dt = parsedate_to_datetime(raw)`; exa:334 `module_dict[_name] = _make_async(_obj)` (brave:21, brave:58, brave:723). Verified: `exa.parsedate_to_datetime` is wrapped; calling it returns `type == _AsyncScalar` (repr datetime(...)); `(wrapped_date) - timedelta(seconds=1)` -> TypeError (only __getattr__ methods like .timestamp() are proxied).
findings.suggestion: Restrict wrapping to functions defined in this module (e.g. `if getattr(_obj, '__module__', None) != <this module>: continue`), and import stdlib helpers with a leading-underscore alias so they stay private. Same fix prevents any future `from X import Y` from being silently re-exported as a wrapped public callable.

findings.lens: DUAL SYNC/ASYNC RESULT WRAPPERS
findings.description: None pass-through is a contract drift. A public function that returns None is boxed in _AsyncScalar(None); the sync caller then receives the proxy, not None, so `result is None` is False (only `not result` is truthy). _AsyncScalar also defers __iter__/__getitem__/__len__/__contains__ straight to None, so those raise TypeError/AttributeError rather than a clean None. Currently latent: no public function in either module returns a bare None (a targeted scan of all wrapped public funcs found none), so this is a latent edge case rather than an active bug — but it will silently break the moment a public fn adds a 'return None' and any caller tests `is None`.
findings.evidence: exa:234-235 / exa:238-261 (_wrap_result fallback `return _AsyncScalar(value)` 'incl. None'; _AsyncScalar.__iter__ -> iter(self._v), __len__ -> len(self._v)). Verified: `w=exa._wrap_result(None); type(w)=='_AsyncScalar'; w is None -> False; bool(w) -> False; iter(w) -> TypeError('NoneType' object is not iterable)`. Scan of all wrapped public functions in exa and brave found no top-level 'return None'.
findings.suggestion: Return None (and ideally other identity-sensitive singletons) untouched from _wrap_result, i.e. add `if value is None: return value` before the generic fallback, so `await fn()` and `fn()` both give exactly None and `is None` checks keep working.

findings.lens: API-KEY AUTH + SECRETS
findings.description: _API_KEY_CACHE is written once per label and never invalidated (no .clear()/.pop()/del anywhere in either module). Once a key is resolved, all later calls in the same process return the cached value and never re-read the environment or key files. A user who rotates/fixes the key mid-process (re-export EXA_API_KEY/BRAVE_API_KEY, or edit the key file) gets the SAME stale key on every subsequent call, so 401s persist and the documented recovery ('export a fresh EXA_API_KEY', 're-export', 're-run /login') silently does not work in-process. This is biting for the intended runtime: exa's docstring (lines 112-113) targets a long-lived IPython agent kernel that reuses the module across many await skill.search(...) calls.

findings.description: Key-store files (~/.prime/agent/keys/exa.key, exa_search_api_key.key, secrets.env, ~/.prime/keys/exa.env, ~/.exa.env — and the PRIME_DOTENV/env files when the dotenv branch misses) are ALWAYS parsed by the naive _read_key_file, never by python-dotenv: the dotenv branch (exa:430-438 / brave:908-917) iterates only the short `files` env-file list, and even when dotenv is installed it is not applied to the key-store files. Consequences for those files: (a) inline comments are not stripped — `EXA_API_KEY=abc # note` yields `abc # note`; (b) `.strip("'\"")` mangles unbalanced quotes ('abc -> abc, "abc -> abc, and strips ALL leading/trailing quote chars); (c) the `len>=12 and "/" not in line` bare-token heuristic treats the first preamble/metadata line that has no '=' and no '/' as the key, a false positive when a key-store file has a header line (>=12 chars) above the real token. python-dotenv is not a declared dependency (both pyproject.toml list only httpx), so the naive parser is the live path in most deployments.

findings.lens: API-KEY AUTH + SECRETS
findings.description: _get_api_key mutates the process environment as a side effect of reading a key: for every key name it runs os.environ.setdefault(n, key), writing the found key into the env even when the user only configured it via a key file or via the *other* name. In brave, _API_KEY_NAMES=['BRAVE_API_KEY','BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY'] and _seek_api_key checks them in order, so a stale BRAVE_API_KEY in the env shadows a correct BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY (first name wins), and setdefault then also pins BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY to that stale value; combined with the never-invalidated cache, unsetting one variable later does not help. Exa (single name) has the same env-mutation smell in a milder form. This is a state-mutation surprise for a library whose only job is to search.
findings.evidence: exa/src/exa/__init__.py:485-486 `for n in _API_KEY_NAMES: os.environ.setdefault(n, key)` (names=['EXA_API_KEY'])  ||  brave/src/brave/__init__.py:964-965 `for n in _API_KEY_NAMES: os.environ.setdefault(n, key)` with 886 `_API_KEY_NAMES = ['BRAVE_API_KEY', 'BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY']` and 893-896 env lookup that returns the first matching name.
findings.suggestion: Do not write back to os.environ from a library (remove the setdefault loop); if a downstream tool genuinely needs the var, document that. For brave, prefer the env var the user actually set over an older sibling, or at least don't cross-populate the two names.

findings.lens: HTTP layer, retry, rate-limit, timeouts
findings.description: exa._request does not catch any transport-level httpx exception. The request call at line 507 is not wrapped in try/except, so httpx.ConnectError/ConnectTimeout/ReadTimeout/PoolTimeout propagate out of _request as raw httpx exceptions with NO retry. This contradicts the docstring (lines 502-500) that 'Transient failures (429 rate-limit, 5xx) are retried up to _retries times with short exponential backoff so a single throttled call does not kill a fan-out.' Only 4xx/5xx status codes (line 518) are retried; a slow response (ReadTimeout at the 45s/60s/90s timeouts used by search/answer/agent) or a connection blip is not retried and surfaces as an unhandled exception to every public caller (search, run, answer, agent, ...).
findings.evidence: lines 506-508: `for attempt in range(_retries + 1):\n        resp = _http().request(method, url, params=params, json=json_body,\n                               headers={"x-api-key": api_key}, timeout=timeout)` (no surrounding try/except); contrast brave lines 991-1008 which wrap the request in `try: ... except (httpx.TimeoutException, httpx.ConnectError, httpx.ConnectTimeout, httpx.ReadTimeout)`.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the _http().request(...) call in try/except for (httpx.TimeoutException, httpx.ConnectError, httpx.ConnectTimeout, httpx.ReadTimeout, httpx.PoolTimeout) and treat it like a transient failure: sleep(_retry_after_seconds(None, 2**attempt*0.5)) and continue within the attempt loop, raising a clean ExaError after exhausting attempts.

findings.lens: HTTP layer, retry, rate-limit, timeouts
findings.description: Non-idempotent stateful requests are blindly re-sent on 429/5xx. _request retries (lines 518-520) apply to every method, including state-creating POST/PATCH/DELETE calls: POST /agent/runs (line 2404, charges agent compute), POST /monitors (line 2998), POST /v0/websets (line 3384), PATCH /monitors/{id} (3019/3216/3917/4014/4018), POST /v0/imports (3950), etc. If a 5xx is returned after the server has already created the resource (or a POST is retried after a 429), the resource can be created twice / billed twice. Even the read endpoints POST /search, /answer, /contents bill per call, so a retried 5xx doubles cost.
findings.evidence: lines 518-520: `if status in (429, 500, 502, 503, 504) and attempt < _retries:\n            time.sleep(_retry_after_seconds(resp, 2 ** attempt * 0.5))\n            continue` (applies regardless of method); line 2404: `created = _request("POST", "/agent/runs", key, json_body=body, timeout=min(timeout, 30))`
findings.suggestion: Only auto-retry idempotent requests, or make _request accept an idempotency signal; for stateful POST/PATCH/DELETE, retry 5xx only when the response indicates the request was not processed, and/or send a client-generated idempotency key on mutating endpoints.

findings.lens: HTTP layer, retry, rate-limit, timeouts
findings.description: Lazy init of the shared process-lifetime httpx.Client and the shared ThreadPoolExecutor is an unlocked check-then-set on a module global, despite the docstring claiming 'thread-safe for request()'. Under concurrent first use (brave batch()/mode='all' _fanout and exa fan-out all submit thread-pool thunks that call _request->_http() at once), two threads can both observe _CLIENT is None and each construct a Client (leaking one, doubling the 16-connection pool briefly); the same pattern applies to _WORKERS, leaking a ThreadPoolExecutor with live threads.
findings.suggestion: Guard lazy init with a module-level threading.Lock (create-once under the lock, then re-check the global), or eagerly create _CLIENT/_WORKERS at import time so the check-then-set race disappears.

This includes _identity_await, _AsyncDict, _AsyncStr, _AsyncList, _AsyncInt, _AsyncFloat, _AsyncBool, _wrap_result, _AsyncScalar, _make_async, _apply_async_to (~200 lines). A `diff` of the two ranges is empty (IDENTICAL). Both also carry the identical module-tail activation call `_apply_async_to(globals())` (exa:5988, brave:7213). Because the copy is verbatim, any bug or fix applied to one copy will silently diverge from the other — the highest-value target for an internal _common module.
findings.evidence: exa 133-137: 'def _identity_await(self): ... if False: # pragma: no cover - makes this a generator (required by await)\n        yield\n    return self' ; exa 140-147 class _AsyncDict(dict) with __await__ returning dict(self) ; exa 216 'def _wrap_result(value):' ; exa 311 'def _apply_async_to(module_dict):' // brave 522-526 identical _identity_await ; brave 529 class _AsyncDict ; brave 605 _wrap_result ; brave 700 _apply_async_to. diff <(sed -n '133,334p' exa/...) <(sed -n '522,723p' brave/...) -> IDENTICAL.
findings.suggestion: Move the whole block into a shared internal module (e.g. search_skills/_common/awaitable.py) and have both exa and brave import it; keep each module's trailing `_apply_async_to(globals())` call pointing at the shared function.

findings.lens: CROSS-MODULE SHARED CODE: exa vs brave helper duplication
findings.description: The API-key lookup trio is byte-identical: exa/__init__.py lines 411-488 vs brave/__init__.py lines 890-967 (_seek_api_key, _read_key_file, _get_api_key). `diff` of each function range is empty (IDENTICAL). The only differences are the module constants that parameterize it: exa has `_API_KEY_NAMES = ['EXA_API_KEY']`, `_API_LABEL = "exa"` (lines 407-408); brave has `_API_KEY_NAMES = ['BRAVE_API_KEY', 'BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY']`, `_API_LABEL = "brave"` (lines 886-887); both define `_API_KEY_CACHE = {}` (exa:409, brave:888). This is credential-resolution logic duplicated across both, so a behavior change or a path/env bug in one copy will not propagate to the other.
findings.evidence:
Both define verbatim: 'def _seek_api_key(names=None):
    from pathlib import Path
    names = names or _API_KEY_NAMES
    for n in names:
        v = os.environ.get(n, "")
        if v and not v.startswith("${"):
            return v ... stem = names[0].split("_")[0].lower() ... return ""' ; 'def _read_key_file(path, names): ... if k.strip() in names and v.strip(): return v.strip().strip("'"\"")' ; 'def _get_api_key(): label = _API_LABEL ... _API_KEY_CACHE[label] = key; return key'. diff of 411-451/890-930, 453-471/932-950, 473-488/952-967 all -> IDENTICAL.
findings.suggestion: Lift the trio into _common with an injected (key_names, label) or a per-skill config object; each module passes its own _API_KEY_NAMES/_API_LABEL. Preserve the per-label _API_KEY_CACHE dict.

findings.lens: CROSS-MODULE SHARED CODE: exa vs brave helper duplication
findings.description: The HTTP-engine core is duplicated with only trivial renames: module globals _ENGINE_LIMITS/_CLIENT/_WORKERS plus _http, _pool, _retry_after_seconds, _fanout. exa 26-79 vs brave 23-80. Bodies are verbatim except: `_http` uses `follow_redirects=True` in exa vs `follow_redirects=False` in brave; `_pool` uses `thread_name_prefix="exa"` vs `"brave"`; `_retry_after_seconds` and `_fanout` differ only in docstring text. Note the intended `follow_redirects` difference means a _common _http must be parameterized, not shared as-is. exa additionally defines `_poll_until` (82-100) which has no brave counterpart, so it is exa-specific. These are small, low-risk duplicates.
findings.evidence: _http: exa line 37 'follow_redirects=True' vs brave line 33 'follow_redirects=False' (rest of body identical). _pool: exa 46 'ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=n, thread_name_prefix="exa")' vs brave 42 'thread_name_prefix="brave"'. _retry_after_seconds diff shows only an added docstring line in brave. _fanout diff shows only differing docstrings; the submit/collect loop (pool.submit / fut.result / try-except append) is identical.
findings.suggestion: Move _ENGINE_LIMITS/_CLIENT/_WORKERS/_http/_pool/_retry_after_seconds/_fanout into _common, making _http take a follow_redirects flag and _pool take a thread_name_prefix. Leave exa's _poll_until in exa (no counterpart in brave).

findings.lens: CROSS-MODULE SHARED CODE: exa vs brave helper duplication
findings.description: Domain/url helpers are CONCEPTUALLY overlapping but DIVERGENT, not near-identical — flagging so a refactor does NOT wrongly merge them. exa `_domain_of` (709-724) computes a registrable domain by stripping scheme/www and slicing the last two labels, and a `hostname` property (693-700) uses urllib.parse.urlparse(...).hostname. brave `_url_host` (114-122) also uses urlparse(...).hostname but lowercases and strips a leading 'www.', and brave `_host` (1081-1084) just reads meta_url.hostname. Same problem space (extract host from a URL), different algorithms and outputs (registrable-domain vs full hostname). The overlap is only the shared `urlparse().hostname` idiom.
findings.evidence: exa 716 'host = url.split("//", 1)[-1].split("/", 1)[0] ... return ".".join(labels[-2:])' (registrable domain) ; exa 698 'urllib.parse.urlparse(u if "://" in u else "https://" + u).hostname' ; brave 119 'host = (urlparse(str(url)).hostname or "").lower()' ; brave 122 'return host[4:] if host.startswith("www.") else host'. No shared function; only the urlparse.hostname idiom matches.
findings.suggestion: Do not fold these into a single shared helper without first unifying the contract (registrable-domain vs host-without-www). If desired, share only a small `urlparse hostname` primitive and keep each module's post-processing separate.
